question: Why is the sky blue during the day but often red or orange at sunset?
answer: Sunlight contains all colours. Air molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen) scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones: Rayleigh scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength. Blue light is therefore scattered all over the sky and reaches your eyes from every direction, so the sky looks blue. Violet is scattered even more, but sunlight contains less violet, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue, so we see blue rather than violet. At sunrise and sunset the light crosses much more air on its longer path to you, so most of the blue is scattered out of the direct beam and the remaining light looks yellow, orange and red. Clouds look white because their droplets are larger than the wavelength of light and scatter all colours about equally (Mie scattering).

Explains sunsets: light crosses a much longer path through the atmosphere, so blue is scattered out and reds/oranges remain

Penalize: says the sky is blue because it reflects the ocean or water
Penalize: says blue light is absorbed (rather than scattered) by the air, or credits ozone/pollution as the main cause of blue sky

question: Explain what causes ocean tides and why most coasts get two high tides a day.
answer: Tides are caused by differences in the gravitational pull of the Moon (and, less strongly, the Sun) across the Earth: the tidal force. It stretches the oceans into two bulges, one on the side facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. As the Earth rotates through both bulges, most coasts get two high and two low tides in each lunar day of about 24 h 50 min, so high tides come roughly 12 h 25 min apart and about 50 minutes later each day. The Sun's tidal force is about 46% of the Moon's. When Sun, Moon and Earth line up (new and full moon) the effects add up and give spring tides with the largest range; at first and third quarter they partly cancel and give neap tides. Coastline shape and water depth strongly change local timing and height.

question: I'm visiting Iceland next month. Why does such a small island have so many volcanoes and hot springs?
answer: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the divergent boundary where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart (about 1.8–1.9 cm per year across the island), so magma rises into the rift zones. It also sits above a mantle hotspot, the Iceland plume, which supplies extra heat and magma and is believed to be why Iceland formed at all. The combination of a spreading ridge and a hotspot gives several active volcanic zones and a lot of heat close to the surface, which feeds the hot springs and geysers.

question: What causes inflation, and why do central banks raise interest rates to fight it?
answer: Inflation is a general rise in the prices of goods and services, which means each unit of money buys less (a fall in purchasing power); it is usually measured with a consumer price index (CPI). Common causes are demand growing faster than the economy can supply (demand-pull), higher production costs such as energy or wages (cost-push), growth in the money supply, and expectations of future inflation that become self-fulfilling. Central banks raise interest rates when inflation is above target because borrowing becomes more expensive and saving more attractive, which cools spending, credit and investment and so eases the pressure on prices; when inflation is below target they lower rates. A 2% target is common among major economies, for example the United States since 2012.

question: Explain Plato's allegory of the cave and what it is meant to illustrate.
answer: In Book VII of the Republic (514a–520a), Socrates describes to Glaucon prisoners chained in a cave so they can only look at the wall in front of them. Behind them burns a fire, and people carry objects whose shadows fall on the wall; the prisoners take the shadows for reality. One prisoner is freed and dragged, painfully, up past the fire and out of the cave, where he sees reflections, then real things, and finally the sun. When he goes back down, his eyes no longer cope with the dark, and the others conclude the journey harmed him; they would kill anyone who tried to drag them out. The allegory illustrates Plato's theory of Forms: the shadows are the world of the senses, the sun stands for the Form of the Good, the ascent is education by reason, and the return is the philosopher's duty to go back and govern even though the others resist.

question: What was the Silk Road, and what besides silk travelled along it?
answer: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes, not a single road, linking China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. It was active from the second century BCE, when the Han dynasty opened it after Zhang Qian's missions (around 114 BCE), until the mid-15th century, and spanned over 6,400 km. The name was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen. Besides silk, merchants carried tea, porcelain, dyes, perfumes, horses, camels, wine and gold, and technologies such as paper and gunpowder. Religions and ideas moved too, Buddhism especially, and so did disease: plague may have travelled the routes and contributed to the Black Death. After 1453, Ottoman control of the overland routes pushed Europeans toward sea routes. In 2014 UNESCO listed the Chang'an–Tianshan corridor as a World Heritage Site.

question: Walk me through how a phone's GPS works out where I am.
answer: GPS uses a constellation of about 31 operational satellites (24 in the baseline design) orbiting at roughly 20,200 km, run by the US Space Force. Each satellite carries atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts its position and the exact time the signal was sent. Your phone's receiver measures when each signal arrives; the delay multiplied by the speed of light gives the distance to that satellite. With distances to at least four satellites, the receiver solves for its three-dimensional position plus its own clock error (three for position, one to correct the cheap clock in the phone). The satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds per day fast relative to clocks on the ground because of relativity, and the system corrects for this. GPS is receive-only: the phone transmits nothing to the satellites and the position fix works without phone or internet reception, although a data connection can speed it up.

question: I'm travelling to Morocco during Ramadan. What is Ramadan, and how does the fast work day to day?
answer: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar and the month of fasting (sawm), one of the Five Pillars of Islam; it commemorates when the Quran was first revealed. It lasts 29 or 30 days, from one sighting of the crescent moon to the next. Each day, observant Muslims abstain from eating, drinking and sexual relations from dawn to sunset. They eat a pre-dawn meal (suhur) and break the fast at sunset with iftar, often a family or community meal. People who are ill, travelling, elderly, pregnant, breastfeeding or menstruating are excused. Because the Islamic calendar is lunar, Ramadan starts about 11 days earlier each solar year and moves through the seasons. It ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr. As a visitor, expect daytime routines and opening hours to shift and evenings to be lively; eating and drinking discreetly in public during daylight is respectful.

question: Why does Earth have seasons?
answer: Because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees relative to its orbit. As Earth goes around the Sun, each hemisphere spends part of the year tilted toward the Sun: the Sun climbs higher in the sky, its rays hit the ground more directly, and days are longer, so that hemisphere has summer. Half a year later the same hemisphere is tilted away: the Sun is low, its energy is spread over a larger area and days are short, so it has winter. That is why the hemispheres have opposite seasons. Distance from the Sun is not the cause: Earth is actually closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January, during the northern winter, and the change in distance alters sunlight intensity by only about 7%.

question: Explain Magna Carta: who forced it on whom in 1215, and why lawyers still cite it.
answer: Magna Carta is the charter King John of England sealed on 15 June 1215 at Runnymede, near Windsor, under pressure from rebel barons; Archbishop Stephen Langton drafted it as a peace deal. Pope Innocent III annulled it within months, and the First Barons' War followed. After John's death it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225 under Henry III, and Edward I confirmed it as statute law in 1297. Its most famous clause (39 in the 1215 text) says no free man shall be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land. It matters because it established the principle that the king is subject to the law, a foundation for due process and the rule of law; it influenced the US Constitution and Bill of Rights. Three clauses are still law in England and Wales (on the freedom of the Church, the liberties of the City of London, and lawful judgement), and four copies of the 1215 charter survive.

question: I'm standing in front of the Rosetta Stone at the British Museum. What exactly is it, and why is it so famous?
answer: It is a granodiorite slab inscribed with a decree issued in 196 BC under King Ptolemy V Epiphanes of Egypt. The same decree appears in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs at the top, Demotic in the middle and Ancient Greek at the bottom. French soldiers found it in July 1799 near the town of Rosetta (Rashid) during Napoleon's campaign in Egypt; after the British defeated the French in 1801 it passed to Britain, and it has been on display at the British Museum almost continuously since 1802. It is famous because scholars could read the Greek, which gave them a key to the hieroglyphs: Thomas Young made early progress, and Jean-François Champollion announced the decipherment in 1822, opening up ancient Egyptian writing. Egypt has asked for it to be returned.

question: If the Sun suddenly vanished, how long would it keep shining in our sky, and why?
answer: About 8 minutes and 20 seconds. Light travels at 299,792,458 m/s, and Earth's mean distance from the Sun (1 astronomical unit) is about 149.6 million km, so sunlight takes roughly 149.6 million km ÷ 300,000 km/s ≈ 499 seconds to reach us. The last light the Sun emitted would still be on its way, so we would keep seeing it for about 8 more minutes before the sky went dark.

question: My flight leaves Tokyo at 9 pm on Monday and takes about 7.5 hours to Honolulu. What day and local time will I land, and how is that possible?
answer: You land at about 9:30 am on Monday, Honolulu time: earlier on the same calendar day than you took off. Tokyo is on UTC+9 and Honolulu on UTC−10, a 19-hour difference, and neither uses daylight saving time. 9 pm Monday in Tokyo is 12:00 UTC Monday; adding 7.5 hours gives 19:30 UTC Monday, which is 09:30 Monday in Honolulu. It is possible because you fly east across the International Date Line, and crossing it eastbound moves the date back by one day.

question: I'm in La Paz, Bolivia, around 3,600 m up, and my pasta takes forever to cook even though the water is boiling hard. Why?
answer: Because at altitude the air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature. The boiling point drops by roughly 1 °F for every 500 ft (152 m) of elevation; at about 3,600 m that is a drop of roughly 24 °F (about 13 °C), so your water boils at around 87 °C instead of 100 °C. Boiling harder does not make the water any hotter; it only evaporates faster. The pasta is cooking at a lower temperature, so it needs more time. Cook it longer, keep a lid on, or use a pressure cooker, which raises the boiling point.

question: Estimate how many years it takes for savings to double at 6% annual interest, and show the shortcut you use.
answer: About 12 years. The rule of 72 says doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ interest rate in percent, so 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. The exact figure with annual compounding is ln 2 ÷ ln 1.06 ≈ 11.9 years, so the shortcut is very close. The rule of 72 works best for rates of roughly 6–10%; for low rates the rule of 70 is closer, and for continuous compounding 69.3. This ignores taxes, fees and inflation, which lower the real growth.

question: Was 1900 a leap year? What about 2000, and why do they differ?
answer: No: 1900 was not a leap year, but 2000 was. Under the Gregorian calendar a year divisible by 4 is a leap year, except century years, which are leap years only if divisible by 400. 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400; 2000 is divisible by 400. The reason is that the tropical year is about 365.2422 days. The Julian calendar's leap day every four years gives 365.25 days, which drifts about three days every 400 years; dropping three leap days per 400 years brings the average to 365.2425 days. Pope Gregory XIII introduced the reform in 1582.

question: I just saw a lightning flash and counted 9 seconds before the thunder. Roughly how far away was the strike, and am I safe where I am outdoors?
answer: About 3 km (roughly 1.8 miles). Light arrives almost instantly, while sound travels about 343 m/s in air, roughly 1 km every 3 seconds or 1 mile every 5 seconds: 9 ÷ 3 ≈ 3 km, or 9 ÷ 5 ≈ 1.8 miles. You are not safe outdoors: if you can hear thunder you are within striking distance. The US National Weather Service advice is 'When thunder roars, go indoors': get into a substantial building with plumbing and wiring, or a hard-topped metal vehicle with the windows closed, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out.

question: On a game show you pick one of three doors; the host, who knows where the car is, opens another door showing a goat and offers a switch. Explain whether you should switch.
answer: Yes, switch: switching wins the car with probability 2/3, staying only 1/3. Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time, so 2/3 of the time the car is behind one of the other two doors. Because the host knows where the car is and always opens a goat door you did not pick, in those 2/3 of cases the one remaining closed door must hide the car. This is the Monty Hall problem, made famous by Marilyn vos Savant's 1990 Parade column. The answer depends on the host's rules: if the host opened a door at random and it merely happened to show a goat, switching and staying would each win 1/2 of the time.

question: How many people do you need in a room for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday?
answer: 23. With 23 people the probability that at least two share a birthday is about 50.7%. It is surprisingly low because what matters is any pair, not a match with one particular person: 23 people form 253 different pairs. With 70 people the probability is about 99.9%. This assumes 365 equally likely birthdays and ignores leap days. By contrast, for a better-than-even chance that someone shares your own birthday you need about 253 people.

question: Did Cleopatra live closer in time to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza or to the first Moon landing?
answer: Closer to the Moon landing. Cleopatra VII lived from 70/69 BC to 30 BC. The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu around 2600–2560 BC, roughly 2,530 years before her death. Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in 1969, about 2,000 years after her death (30 BC to AD 1969 is 1,998 years, as there is no year zero). So she lived about 500 years closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramid's construction.

question: Work out roughly how many Earths could fit inside the Sun, using their diameters.
answer: About 1.3 million. The Sun's diameter is about 1,391,400 km, roughly 109 times Earth's. Volume scales with the cube of the diameter, so the volume ratio is about 109³ ≈ 1.3 million. (If you packed solid Earth-sized balls inside, gaps would mean fewer would fit, but by volume it is ~1.3 million.) By mass the Sun is only about 330,000 Earths, because it is much less dense on average.

question: I'm flying across Australia and a friend said it's about the same size as the United States. Which is actually bigger?
answer: The United States is bigger: about 9.83 million km² against Australia's about 7.69 million km². Your friend is roughly right only for the contiguous 48 states (about 8.08 million km² of total area), which are comparable to Australia but still about 5% larger. The gap for the whole country comes mostly from Alaska. Australia is the world's sixth-largest country; the US ranks around fourth.

question: Compare Stoicism and Epicureanism: what each school saw as the goal of life and how they told people to live.
answer: Both are Hellenistic schools founded in Athens around 300 BC. Stoicism, founded by Zeno of Citium (taught at the Stoa Poikile), held that virtue is the only true good and that a flourishing life (eudaimonia) comes from living in agreement with nature and reason. It stressed focusing on what is in your control (your own judgements and actions), transforming destructive passions into rational feelings, and taking part in public life and duty; later Roman Stoics include Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. Epicureanism, founded by Epicurus in 307 BC at his Garden in Athens, held that pleasure is the goal, but understood pleasure as tranquillity (ataraxia) and absence of bodily pain (aponia), reached through modest living, friendship and freedom from fear. Epicureans were atomists, thought the gods do not intervene in the world, taught that 'death is nothing to us', and advised withdrawing from politics. Key contrast: for Stoics virtue is the end itself; for Epicureans virtue is a means to a pleasant, untroubled life.

question: How do viruses and bacteria differ, and why does that matter for treatment?
answer: A bacterium is a single-celled living organism (a prokaryote): it has its own cell membrane and cell wall, carries out its own metabolism and reproduces by itself by dividing (binary fission). Most bacteria are harmless or useful, for example in the gut, but some cause disease, such as tuberculosis or cholera. A virus is much smaller (more than a thousand bacteriophage viruses could fit inside one bacterium) and is not a cell: it is genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat (capsid), sometimes with a lipid envelope, and it can only replicate inside the living cells of a host. Whether viruses count as alive is debated. Practically, antibiotics work against bacteria but have no effect on viruses; viral infections such as colds and flu are handled with antiviral drugs, vaccines and the immune system.

question: I've climbed Mount Fuji and now I'm thinking about Mont Blanc. How much higher is Mont Blanc, and why do sources give different heights for it?
answer: Mont Blanc is roughly 1,030 m higher. Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain and an active stratovolcano, is 3,776 m. Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in the Alps, on the France–Italy border, was measured at 4,807.3 m in the 2025 survey (4,805.59 m in 2023). Its height varies because the summit is a thick dome of ice and snow whose thickness changes with weather and seasons, so there is no exact permanent summit elevation; older figures such as 4,808 m or 4,810 m reflect earlier measurements.

question: Compare the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire: who held power, and when did one become the other?
answer: The Republic ran from about 509 BC, when the monarchy was overthrown, to 27 BC. Power was spread among elected officials: two consuls elected each year who could veto each other, other magistrates, the Senate of leading families, and popular assemblies, with a dictator appointed only for emergencies. Rome already ruled most of the Mediterranean under the Republic. After decades of civil war, Julius Caesar's assassination in 44 BC, and Octavian's victory over Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BC, the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus on 16 January 27 BC, the conventional start of the Empire. Under the Empire (the Principate), the emperor held real power, above all command of the army, while republican institutions such as the Senate continued in form. The Western Empire ended in AD 476; the Eastern Empire lasted until 1453.
rubric: Republic: elected consuls (two, annual), Senate, assemblies; from ~509 BC

Empire: emperor holds real power while the Senate continues in form
Penalize: names Julius Caesar as the first emperor
Penalize: says the Republic had a king or that the Senate was abolished under the Empire

question: How do nuclear fission and nuclear fusion differ, and which one do commercial nuclear power plants run on?
answer: Fission splits a heavy nucleus, such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239, into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons that can split further nuclei in a chain reaction. It was discovered in 1938 by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann and explained by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch. Commercial nuclear power plants run on fission (as do atomic bombs), and it produces long-lived radioactive waste. Fusion joins light nuclei, such as the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium, into a heavier one (helium); it powers the Sun and other stars. It needs extreme temperatures and pressures (millions of degrees) to overcome the repulsion between nuclei, and it releases more energy per unit of mass than fission. The US National Ignition Facility got more fusion energy out than laser energy in for the first time in December 2022, but no commercial fusion power plant operates; projects such as ITER are still being built.

Commercial power plants use fission; fusion power is still experimental

Penalize: claims commercial fusion electricity already exists

question: I'm moving from a country run by a president to one run by a prime minister. How does a parliamentary system differ from a presidential one?
answer: In a parliamentary system the executive (a cabinet led by a prime minister) comes from and is accountable to the legislature: it governs only while it keeps the confidence of a parliamentary majority and can be removed by a vote of no confidence, after which it must resign or call an election. Executive and legislature are fused rather than separated, and the head of state (a monarch or a largely ceremonial president) is usually a different person from the head of government; examples are the UK, Germany and India. In a presidential system the president is both head of state and head of government, is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term, and cannot be removed by the legislature except through impeachment; powers are separated, as in the United States or Brazil. Trade-off: parliamentary governments can be replaced quickly; presidential systems give a stable executive but can deadlock when president and legislature disagree. Some countries, such as France, mix the two (semi-presidential).

question: What is the Bitcoin halving, and how has the block reward changed since 2009?
answer: The halving is the built-in rule that cuts the new-bitcoin subsidy paid to miners per block in half every 210,000 blocks, which at about one block per 10 minutes is roughly every four years. The reward started at 50 BTC in 2009, fell to 25 BTC in 2012, 12.5 BTC in 2016, 6.25 BTC in 2020 and 3.125 BTC in April 2024; the next halving, expected around 2028, will cut it to 1.5625 BTC. Because the subsidy keeps halving, total issuance approaches a hard cap of 21 million BTC. Miners also earn transaction fees, which become relatively more important as the subsidy shrinks.

question: Explain what Ethereum's Merge changed and what it did not change.
answer: On 15 September 2022 (the Paris upgrade) Ethereum's original execution layer merged with the Beacon Chain, the proof-of-stake chain running since 1 December 2020. Proof-of-work mining ended; blocks are now proposed and attested by validators who stake ETH, and Ethereum's energy use dropped by about 99.95%. What it did not change: it did not lower gas fees (it changed the consensus mechanism, not network capacity); it did not enable withdrawals of staked ETH, which came with the Shanghai/Capella upgrade on 12 April 2023; and it barely changed transaction speed (12-second slots versus about 13.3-second blocks before). Users did not need to do anything, and balances and history stayed the same.

question: My phone with my crypto wallet app just got stolen. I still have the 12-word recovery phrase I wrote down. Are my coins gone, and what should I do?
answer: Probably not. Your coins are recorded on the blockchain, not stored on the phone. The 12-word recovery (seed) phrase, usually a BIP39 phrase drawn from a list of 2,048 words, holds all the information needed to recreate your wallet's keys. Install a compatible wallet app on another device and restore the wallet with the phrase; if you think the phone or the phrase may be compromised, move the funds to a new wallet with a new phrase. Keep the phrase offline and never share it or type it into a website: anyone who has it controls your funds, and no legitimate support agent or service will ever ask for it, so treat any message asking for it, for example from 'wallet support', as a scam.

question: What did EIP-1559 change about Ethereum transaction fees?
answer: EIP-1559, activated in the London upgrade on 5 August 2021, replaced the old first-price auction, where each user just bid a single gas price. Each block now has a protocol-set base fee per unit of gas that every transaction must pay and that is burned (destroyed) rather than paid to the block producer; users add an optional priority fee (tip) for the block producer, set a maximum fee they are willing to pay, and get the difference refunded. Blocks became variable in size around a target of half the gas limit, and the base fee rises or falls by up to 12.5% per block depending on whether the previous block was above or below that target. The goal was more predictable fees that wallets can estimate reliably, not permanently lower fees.

question: Compare optimistic rollups and zk-rollups on how they prove correctness and how long withdrawals to Ethereum take.
answer: Both execute transactions off-chain and post batches to Ethereum. Optimistic rollups assume batches are valid and publish no proof; during a challenge period of about seven days anyone can dispute a result with a fraud proof. As a result, withdrawals back to Ethereum must wait out that one-week window (liquidity providers can pay you out sooner for a fee). ZK-rollups attach a validity proof (a SNARK or STARK) to each batch, which a contract on Ethereum verifies; once the proof is verified, withdrawals can be executed with no challenge delay. Trade-offs: producing validity proofs is computationally heavy and can require specialised hardware, EVM compatibility is harder to build, SNARKs need a trusted setup, and STARKs avoid it at the cost of larger proofs.

question: A friend told me Bitcoin is anonymous, so nobody can trace what I buy with it. Is that right?
answer: No. Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Every transaction is public, traceable and permanently recorded on the blockchain; bitcoin.org calls Bitcoin 'probably the most transparent payment network in the world'. Your addresses are not labelled with your name, but once any of them is linked to you (for example because you had to identify yourself to buy goods or services, or you posted an address publicly), your past and future transactions can be followed, and chain analysis can group addresses that appear to share an owner. Using a new address for each payment helps privacy but does not make Bitcoin anonymous.

question: I've had a cold with a runny nose and sore throat for three days. Should I ask my doctor for antibiotics?
answer: Usually not. Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only work against bacteria: the NHS says they do not work for viral infections such as colds and flu, or most coughs, and they are no longer routinely prescribed for sore throats. They will not speed up your recovery, and taking them when they are not needed can cause side effects and makes antibiotic resistance more likely. Most people start to feel better in about 1 to 2 weeks with rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches or fever. See a doctor if a high temperature lasts more than 3 days, symptoms suddenly get worse, you are short of breath or have chest pain, symptoms do not improve after 10 days, a cough lasts more than 3 weeks, or you have a long-term condition or weakened immune system.

question: How many hours of sleep do adults need each night?
answer: The CDC recommends 7 or more hours a night for adults aged 18 to 60, 7–9 hours for ages 61 to 64, and 7–8 hours for those 65 and older; teenagers (13 to 17) need 8–10 hours. Regularly sleeping less is linked with type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, stroke, car crashes and poorer thinking and concentration. To sleep better: keep a consistent schedule, keep the bedroom cool and quiet, avoid screens for at least 30 minutes before bed, limit caffeine and alcohol in the evening, and exercise regularly.

question: Explain what the SPF number on sunscreen means and how to use sunscreen properly.
answer: SPF (sun protection factor) measures how much protection a sunscreen gives against ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation. It says nothing about UVA, which is shown separately; in the UK by a star rating. The NHS recommends a sunscreen with at least SPF 30 and at least 4-star UVA protection. Use enough, about 6 to 8 teaspoons to cover an adult's whole body, and reapply it every 2 hours, because the sun dries it off, and straight after swimming, sweating or towelling. Check the expiry: the open-jar symbol with a number and 'M' shows how many months it lasts once opened. Do not rely on sunscreen alone: spend time in the shade when the sun is strongest (11am to 3pm in the UK from March to October), and cover up with clothing, a hat and sunglasses.

question: I'm flying from London to Tokyo, eight or nine time zones ahead. How can I reduce jet lag, and how long will it last?
answer: Jet lag happens because your body clock is still on London time. The NHS says it usually improves within a few days as you adjust; full adjustment is often estimated at about one day per time zone crossed, and eastward trips like this one are usually harder because your body has to shift earlier. Before you go, move your bedtime and wake-up time gradually earlier over a few days. On the flight, drink plenty of water, go easy on alcohol and caffeine, and try to sleep if it is night time in Tokyo. After you land, switch to the local schedule straight away, get outside in daylight, since natural light helps your body clock adjust, and avoid napping during the day. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using sleeping tablets or melatonin.

question: I'm in a beachfront café on a coast that gets tsunamis, and the ground starts shaking hard. What should I do during the shaking and right after it stops?
answer: During the shaking: Drop, Cover and Hold On. Drop onto your hands and knees, cover your head and neck (under a sturdy table if one is close), and hold on until the shaking stops. Do not run outside while the ground is shaking, and avoid doorways. As soon as the shaking stops, because you are on a tsunami coast, treat the strong shaking itself as a warning: move immediately inland or to high ground, as high and as far as you can (Ready.gov suggests 100 feet above sea level or at least a mile inland). Do not wait for an official warning or siren. Other natural signs are a sudden rise or draining of the sea that exposes the sea floor, or a loud roar from the ocean. A tsunami is a series of waves, so stay on high ground and follow local authorities' instructions. Away from the coast you would normally stay where you are after the shaking, but here getting to high ground fast comes first.

question: The power has been out for a day. Can I run my portable generator in the attached garage if I keep the big door open?
answer: No. The CDC says never use a generator inside your home or garage, even if doors and windows are open. Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide (CO), a colourless, odourless gas that can kill within minutes. Run the generator outside only, more than 20 feet (about 6 m) from windows, doors and vents (Ready.gov adds: away from attached garages), and install battery-powered CO alarms near sleeping areas. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea or vomiting, chest pain and confusion. If anyone has symptoms or a CO alarm sounds, get everyone outside into fresh air at once, do not go back in, and call emergency services (911 in the US, 999 in the UK), especially for breathing difficulty, confusion or loss of consciousness.

question: Explain how first aid differs for a hypothermic person who is shivering but fully alert, compared with one who has become drowsy, confused or unconscious.
answer: In both cases treat hypothermia as an emergency: the NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 if you think someone has it, and the CDC says to get medical attention immediately if body temperature is below 95 °F (35 °C). While help comes, get the person into a warm room or shelter, remove wet clothing, wrap them in blankets, and warm the centre of the body first: chest, neck, head and groin. Skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry layers also helps. If they are shivering but fully awake, give a warm non-alcoholic drink and some sugary food such as chocolate, and keep talking to them. If they are drowsy, confused or unconscious, call emergency services at once and do not give them anything to drink, since they could choke. Check their breathing; if they stop breathing or have no pulse, start CPR, even if they appear dead, because hypothermia victims can sometimes be revived. For everyone, avoid a hot bath, hot-water bottles or heat lamps, do not rub their arms, legs, hands or feet, and never give alcohol.

question: What's the difference between heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and at what point should I call 999 or 911?
answer: Heat exhaustion is the body struggling with heat and loss of water and salt: heavy sweating, pale and clammy skin, headache, dizziness, feeling or being sick, cramps, tiredness, a high temperature and strong thirst. Move the person somewhere cool, remove unnecessary clothing, give plenty of water or a sports drink, and cool their skin by spraying or sponging with cool water and fanning. They should start to feel better within 30 minutes. Heatstroke is when the body can no longer control its temperature. It is a medical emergency, with a very high temperature, hot skin that may stop sweating, a fast heartbeat, confusion or slurred speech, seizures or loss of consciousness. Call 999 or 911 if the person is still unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, or at once if there are signs of heatstroke. While waiting, keep cooling them fast (cold water or an ice bath if possible, cold wet cloths, soaking their clothes) and stay with them. If they are unconscious, do not give them anything to drink: put them in the recovery position and watch their breathing.

question: I'm driving at night and the road ahead dips under moving floodwater that looks only a few inches deep. Is it safe to drive through slowly?
answer: No. Turn around, don't drown. Ready.gov warns that just 6 inches (15 cm) of moving water can knock a person down and 1 foot (30 cm) of moving water can sweep a vehicle away, and at night you cannot judge the depth, the current or whether the road underneath has washed out. Turn around, find another route, or wait on higher ground until the water goes down. Do not walk or swim through the water either. If your car does get trapped in rapidly moving water, stay inside; if water rises inside the car, get onto the roof and call for help.

question: My teacher said Einstein got his Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity. Which year did he win it for relativity?
answer: He didn't: the premise is wrong. Einstein never received a Nobel Prize for relativity. question: Why did Viking warriors wear horned helmets into battle?
answer: They didn't. There is no evidence that Viking warriors wore horned helmets. Viking Age texts mention helmets but never horns, and the Viking-era helmets archaeologists have found have no horns. The image is a 19th-century invention, popularised by productions of Richard Wagner's operas. The only Scandinavian horned helmets known, the Veksø helmets, date from the Bronze Age, more than a thousand years before the Vikings, and were probably ceremonial.

question: Tell me who invented the wheel and the exact year it happened.
answer: That can't be answered as asked: the inventor of the wheel is unknown and there is no exact year. What archaeology shows is a range. Potter's wheels go back to the middle of the 5th millennium BCE (Cucuteni–Trypillia culture), pictographs of wheeled wagons from Uruk in Mesopotamia date to about 3500–3350 BCE, and the oldest wooden wheel found, the Ljubljana Marshes Wheel in Slovenia, dates to about 3200–3100 BCE. The wheel probably developed in several regions (Mesopotamia, the Northern Caucasus, Central Europe) rather than coming from one inventor.

question: I'm planning a trip to San Francisco. On what date will the next big earthquake hit there, so I can avoid it?
answer: Nobody can tell you: earthquakes cannot be predicted. question: Why did the Western Roman Empire fall?
answer: There is no single cause, and historians still debate it. The conventional end date is AD 476, when the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. Major factors: migrations and invasions, with Goths pushed west by the Huns and the disastrous defeat at Adrianople in 378, where Emperor Valens died; the sacks of Rome by the Visigoths (410) and the Vandals (455); the loss of the rich North African provinces to the Vandals in 439, which cut the tax base needed to pay the army; repeated civil wars and usurpations; economic strain and inflation; plague and climate deterioration; and the division into eastern and western halves, with the wealthier, better-defended East surviving until 1453. Edward Gibbon (1776) framed it as decline and fall; many modern historians see a gradual transformation rather than a sudden collapse.

question: Explain what caused the Black Death and how it changed European society afterwards.
answer: The Black Death (1346–1353) was a pandemic of plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It spread mainly through flea bites (fleas on rats, and probably human fleas and body lice), while the pneumonic form passed directly from person to person. It came from Central Asia and reached Europe via Crimea and Genoese merchant ships that brought it to Sicily. It killed an estimated 25–50 million people in Europe, 30–60% of the population, with higher totals of 75–200 million proposed for Eurasia and North Africa, although the toll varied by region. Afterwards, the shortage of workers pushed wages up and weakened serfdom and the feudal system. Jews and other minorities were persecuted and blamed for the disease, and religious life changed, with many people turning to more intense and more personal forms of piety.

question: I'm reading about the Industrial Revolution. Why did it start in Britain rather than somewhere else?
answer: It began in Britain around 1760 (running to about 1820–1840) because several conditions came together there. Britain had abundant coal and iron, plus water power, close to an extensive network of ports, navigable rivers, canals and roads. The agricultural revolution raised farm productivity, freeing labour for industry and producing food surpluses. Political stability, a legal system favourable to business, patents that protected inventions, and access to financial capital let entrepreneurs invest, and there were skilled managers and entrepreneurs to do it. Overseas trade and colonial expansion, including the trade in cotton textiles, gave access to raw materials and markets. On top of this came key inventions in textiles, such as the spinning jenny and the water frame, and the steam engine. Historians still argue about how much weight each factor deserves; no single one explains it.

question: I'm bringing my American 120-volt hair dryer to London. Will it work with just a plug adapter?
answer: Not safely, unless it is dual-voltage. The UK uses 230 V at 50 Hz with Type G plugs (three rectangular pins); the US uses 120 V at 60 Hz with Type A/B plugs. A plug adapter only changes the shape of the plug, not the voltage. Plugging a 120 V-only device into 230 V can badly damage it, and a hair dryer may overheat or even catch fire. Check the label: if it says something like 100–240 V, or has a 110/220 V switch (set it to 220–240), a plug adapter alone will do. Otherwise either use a voltage converter rated above the dryer's wattage, which is hard for a high-power heating appliance, or simply get a dual-voltage or UK dryer. Phone and laptop chargers are usually 100–240 V and need only an adapter.

question: Explain how the Schengen 90/180-day rule works for visa-exempt visitors and how to count my days.
answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors may stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period in the Schengen Area, which counts as a single area: days in every Schengen country add up together, not per country. The 180-day window is rolling and backward-looking. On any day of your stay, count back 180 days and add up the days you spent in the Schengen Area; the total must not go over 90. Days spent in countries outside Schengen (for example Ireland or the UK) do not count, and leaving the area does not reset the count; old days only drop out as they fall outside the 180-day window. The European Commission has an online short-stay calculator for checking dates. Overstaying can lead to fines and entry bans; to stay longer you need a national long-stay visa or residence permit.

question: What are the ways to reach Machu Picchu from Cusco, and is there a road all the way?
answer: There is no road all the way: the town below the ruins, Aguas Calientes, can only be reached by train or on foot. Most people take a PeruRail or Inca Rail train from the Cusco area (Poroy or San Pedro station) or from Ollantaytambo in the Sacred Valley to Aguas Calientes. From there a bus climbs the switchbacks to the site in about 30 minutes, or you can walk up a steep path in about 1½–2 hours. Hiking options include the government-controlled Inca Trail (four-day and two-day versions, with daily limits, so book well ahead) and the Salkantay trek. The budget 'back door' route goes by minivan via Santa María and Santa Teresa to Hidroeléctrica, then 2–3 hours on foot to Aguas Calientes. Entry tickets are limited and not sold at the gate, so buy them in advance, and bring your passport.
rubric: No road to Aguas Calientes: train or on foot
Train (PeruRail/Inca Rail) from Cusco/Poroy or Ollantaytambo; bus (~30 min) or walk up from Aguas Calientes
Alternatives: Inca Trail (permits, limits), Salkantay, Hidroeléctrica back route
Practical: buy entry tickets in advance, passport required
